content.text: Prahlada, the illustrious son of the Daitya king Hiranyakasipu, resided as a boy in the dwelling of his preceptor, where he read such writings as are studied in early years. Brought before his father and asked to repeat what he had learned, Prahlada answered: ‘I have learned to adore him who is without beginning, middle, or end, increase or diminution; the imperishable lord of the world, the universal cause of causes.’ When his father demanded who had taught him this, Prahlada replied, ‘Vishnu, father, is the instructor of the whole world: what else should any one teach or learn, save him the supreme spirit?’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: Enraged, Hiranyakasipu cried ‘Kill the wretch! he is not fit to live,’ and his attendants rushed upon Prahlada with weapons. The prince calmly said: ‘Daityas, as truly as Vishnu is present in your weapons and in my body, so truly shall those weapons fail to harm me’; and though struck heavily and repeatedly by hundreds of the Daityas, Prahlada felt not the least pain, and his strength was ever renewed.
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: Hiranyakasipu next commanded the great snakes Kuhaka, Takshaka, and Andhaka to bite his son with their envenomed fangs; but Prahlada, his thoughts immovably fixed on Krishna, felt no pain, and the snakes cried out to the king, ‘Our fangs are broken... but the skin of the youth is still unscathed.’ Then elephants of the skies were sent to gore and trample him, but their tusks were blunted against his breast; Prahlada said, ‘Calling upon Janarddana is my defence against such fearful affliction.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: The king then ordered a mighty heap of wood piled around the prince and set alight. But Prahlada cried, ‘Father, this fire, though blown up by the winds, burneth me not; and all around I behold the face of the skies, cool and fragrant, with beds of lotus flowers.’ Priests who witnessed this pleaded with Hiranyakasipu to restrain his wrath against his own son, and the prince was liberated from the flames.
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: Returned to his preceptor's house, Prahlada gave lessons to the sons of the demons in the intervals of his leisure: ‘Sons of the offspring of Diti, hear from me the supreme truth... Birth, infancy, and youth are the portion of all creatures; and then succeeds gradual and inevitable decay... Verily I say unto you, that in this ocean of the world, this sea of many sorrows, Vishnu is your only hope... Let all your thoughts and affections be fixed on him, who is present in all beings, and you shall laugh at every care.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: Meditating upon Vishnu as identical with his own spirit, Prahlada became as one with him, and in consequence the bonds with which he was bound burst instantly asunder; the ocean was violently uplifted, and the prince, putting aside the rocks the demons had piled upon him, came forth from out the main. He hymned Purushottama: ‘Om! glory to the end of all: to thee, lord, who art subtile and substantial; mutable and immutable; perceptible and imperceptible... Oh thou who art both one and many, Vasudeva, first cause of all; glory be unto thee.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: When Vishnu appeared before him and offered a boon, Prahlada asked not for his own sake but for his father's: ‘I have been hated, for that I assiduously proclaimed thy praise: do thou, oh lord, pardon in my father this sin that he hath committed... do thou therefore free my father from this iniquity.’ After Hiranyakasipu was slain by Vishnu in the form of the man-lion (Narasimha), Prahlada became the sovereign of the Daityas, ruling with the splendours of piety, and the text promises that whoever hears his history is cleansed from sin.
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

content.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Horace Hayman Wilson's 1840 translation of the Vishnu Purana, Book I, Chapters XVII ('Legend of Prahlada') and XX ('Vishnu appears to Prahlada'), fetched directly from sacred-texts.com's hosting of this public-domain translation (Wilson died 1860; the translation itself is unambiguously public domain). Chapters XVIII–XIX, covering the intervening trials (being cast from a cliff, poisoned, bound and thrown into the sea), were not directly fetched in this batch and are therefore not quoted here, though referenced only in general terms via the app's existing figure summary.
